utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. If I could remind you, Mr. Brolund, that you are still subject to the affirmation you took yesterday. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brolund, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In connection with the meeting at Meljine on the 28th of October, 1991, can you tell me if you had any role to play, or a task at that meeting? Did you speak at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that I did not speak at that meeting at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The document containing the proposals for normalisation of life in Dubrovnik is dated the 25th of October, 1991, and you came to the meeting on the 28th of October, 1991. Did you see this document at all? Was it presented at the meeting that day?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At the meeting in Meljine, were the single items of these -- of this document individually discussed?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to recall to what extent there was a detailed discussion about the single points.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you know the detailed answers, in view of the fact that only three days had gone by, and were you familiar with the proposals of the Croatian side concerning this document?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the purpose of your mission, going to Meljine with Ambassador Bondioli, was for him to meet General Strugar, for the sake of courtesy?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Following the meeting, did you ever ask or did you get to know how many other times the Croatian side and the JNA had met, and what, if any, agreements they had reached?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't any knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the room where the meeting was held, did General Strugar strike you as the oldest representative of the JNA being there, the most senior one?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you describe to us today what Admiral Jokic looks like?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember at all Admiral Jokic from that meeting. I know only that he was present there due to my notes. But I remember him very clearly from later on, or relatively clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember, who spoke more at the meeting, General Strugar or Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a long meeting, and I'm not able to establish, it seems to me, who did speak most. Both General Strugar and Admiral Jokic did talk much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Admiral Jokic, was he introduced at the meeting as the commander of the navy, based in Boka?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I have nothing about that in my notes, and, as I said before, I can't recall that he was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the meeting on the 28th of October.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, certainly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was Admiral Jokic present?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said a couple of times, I can't recall in my memory that he was present. I know that he was present only due to my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As for the period of time you spent in Dubrovnik when you took part in these various meetings, do you have any idea what Admiral Jokic's position was or which branch of the army he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could see also on his uniform that he did belong to the navy, but exactly which position he had, that is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was there any difference between Admiral Jokic and Jeremic, who also attended the meeting wearing a navy-blue uniform, representing the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only difference I noticed was the difference in rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, 1991, on that day, where were you exactly, between morning and evening?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our team, all members of our team, including myself, we were in the Hotel Argentina on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where were you specifically staying at the hotel on that day? Which section of the hotel? The cellar, perhaps? Any other room, your own room? Tell us more about this, please.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the shelling began, so about 6.00 in the morning, I was in my room, and after having heard that something was going on, I went down to the operations room, which was in the lowest floor, you can say, in the cellar of the building, towards the sea. And there we stayed most of the day. We could go out on the veranda outside. This room towards the sea, and from there we could watch, more or less, the Old Town, and we could also, for example, see our own boats. So in this room we were most of the time, but a couple of times I also, for example, went up to my own room.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. In the course of that day, the 6th of December, were there any operations being carried out by the Croatian forces out of Dubrovnik? And I'm referring to the general area of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not able to establish anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did any information reach you in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You stated that on the 8th of December there were two officers who came to visit the Old Town, to carry out an inspection of the damage that had occurred on the 6th of December; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How were you in a position to know that those were two JNA officers? Based on what?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got that information from the Croatian officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you get any more specific information as for the description of the people, the JNA people who came to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Will you please open your own notes.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I think we're talking about the last page, and the date is the 8th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please read to us from your own handwriting what exactly it reads, just underneath the date saying the 8th of December.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Before noon, we escorted JNA photographers and 'intelligence agents' who did inspect the damages in Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Therefore, a JNA photograph and an intelligence officer. Can you please clarify this? How did you get this information? You said that the Croatian side had informed you that only two JNA officers would be coming.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. As I told yesterday, yesterday and also today, I'm not able to establish, to recall how many persons there were all together. When I made my statement two years ago, I said that there were two officers, and I'm sure that at that time I could recall that. But today I'm not able to establish how many persons there were all together and what their functions were. And I want to draw your attention to the fact that the word "intelligence agents" is in inverted commas, so with this word, I just indicate that it was not completely clear to me how some representatives of the JNA could come into the town like this and which function they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I assume it should be clear to you that they had reached the town, pursuant to an agreement with the monitoring mission itself and the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember how much the mission took part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Had you ever seen any JNA officers walking around Dubrovnik before, or had you ever had any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, during your testimony yesterday you also said that you had given a statement to the Tribunal investigators using your notes, because you were not able to remember all those developments without consulting your notes. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had these notes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you give your statement mostly based on your notes?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, concerning a lot of details, yes, because I was not able to remember many details after such a long time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask the usher to please give the witness statement to all the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask the purpose of it? Witness statements are neither documentary evidence, nor evidence of any kind. What is the purpose of the examination, or of the presentation of the document? However would it help?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order to finish my cross-examination as soon as possible, I want to have this statement distributed to everyone so everyone can follow, in order to better understand the questions that I'm asking. And I'm sure that I will eventually tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're going to cross-examine on the statement, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I will allow that, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this the statement you gave the investigators of the Tribunal 2002? And the signature on the statement, is it your signature?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my statement and my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I will ask you to please go to page 4 of your statement, second passage, halfway down the passage. I will read it out, and you, please, if you can, follow. "About 3.00 p.m., we got information from Jokic. This was an excuse to do with the shelling." Is this what you wrote? Is that part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Will you please now open your own notes as they relate to the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. May I just ask indulgence to request that it be read completely correctly from the statement in English, which is not what is on the screen. I note that what is on the screen is: "I noted that approximately 1500, we received word from Jokic with an excuse about the shelling." That differs from what is on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. I think you're quite right there, Ms. Somers. It's with "an excuse about the shelling" rather than as it was read to the transcript, when the words used were "with an excuse to do with the shelling." I think the transcript will record the difference now. Thank you. If you'd carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. My apologies, Your Honour. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at your notes now, your notes of the 6th of December. It's towards the bottom of the page. There is a statement made at 3.00 p.m. The two lines, the one which begins "3.00 p.m." And the next line, which begins with the word "Jokic." Can you please read out exactly what you wrote.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that. "1500 hours, shelling still going on, though Admiral Jokic sent excuse."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on page 4, fourth passage, can you please have a look. It's about the meeting that was held on the 7th of December. Can you please find the sentence which says that during the meeting, a strong objection was made by Mr. Hvalkof. Can you please find that sentence, in passage 4.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please read that sentence and the three sentences following that sentence.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: "During or after the meeting, I interpreted a strong protest from Hvalkof concerning the December 6th shelling. I don't recall the exact responses Jokic made relating to the protest. I got the impression he appeared sorry about what had happened but did not actually make any apology. I don't remember him making any excuses for any of the JNA units. We subsequently returned to Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this what happened?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me -- you can leave your statement now. At the moment, in The Hague, do you have with you the original copy of your notes and the photographs that we were shown yesterday in Court?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not of the photographs, but I have of the notes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The notes you have in front of you now, is this the original copy?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think most of it is here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let's try to be specific about this. The notes you have read from yesterday and today in Court, are these notes the original copy of your notes, or are they the original copy of the notes, with no exceptions? I think the question is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the originals here, or perhaps one part of it in my luggage. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So what we have here in the courtroom are copies of your original copy?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I have all originals here in the courtroom, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I want to make sure you understand me correctly. The sheets of paper there you have in front of you now, these notes, is this the original or is this merely a copy?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a copy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: These photographs, these four photographs that have been tendered into evidence, P24, were these taken between the 4th and the 8th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon? Could I have a look at the photos? The first photo from Cavtat is taken on the 5th of December, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you right away: The text below the photograph, whose handwriting is that?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me about the next photograph? Was it also taken during the same period as the first one and the remaining two?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is not -- this photo with the armoured vehicle is not from the same period. It is obviously from my first stay at Dubrovnik, so between the 5th and the 10th of October. Because my colleague, Leif Maersk, is also on the photo. And I was -- when the investigators visited me --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not even completely sure about the origin of that photo, if it is from Dubrovnik or from another place, but it seems to me that it is from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. What can we see in this second photograph?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that it's quite a sort of homemade, in inverted commas, armoured vehicle, with the Croatian signs on it. So it seems to be belonging to the Croatian armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this vehicle armed? On the turret, one can see weapons.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the photo is not so good, but probably there is some -- perhaps a machine-gun or something on the top of it. I'm not able to establish that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I have to conclude, however, that when responding to my questions, you said that in early October, when these photographs were taken, on the occasion of your first visit to Dubrovnik, you did not see any members of the Croatian army or anything to do with the military, the Croatian military. Thank you. When preparing for your testimony of yesterday, did you use your notes?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have used these notes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When did you arrive in The Hague in order to testify?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th, Sunday, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The day before your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to anyone from the Office of the Prosecutor in connection with your testimony of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon? Could I have the question once more?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to any representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, an investigator or a Prosecution counsel, when preparing for your testimony of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Already on the 18th, in the evening, I had a so-called proofing with the counsellor, with the Prosecutor, and that continued on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me -- I do apologise. On that occasion, did the representatives of the OTP give you the copy of the notes that you have in front of you, the copy of your notes? Because you don't have the original with you in the courtroom. I see that you have the same copies I have. Did they give you these copies?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me now: Who highlighted parts of the text in these notes for you with a highlighter?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the day before yesterday, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is there anything in these notes relating to the period of your work in Dubrovnik that would represent an important event in that period but is not highlighted or mentions a person you met - I'm referring to representatives of the JNA - which is not highlighted?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now I'm not able to establish or remember what I have been highlighting and what not. I just highlighted some important parts of the text so it would be easier for me to orientate myself in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was what you were going to be asked about highlighted by the Office of the Prosecutor? Is that what you highlighted?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could not know what I would be asked. I highlighted this myself on Sunday evening, and on Monday morning, just for my own purposes, in order to -- when I read it through, in order to -- so I could easily orientate myself in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the answer to most of the questions I put to you yesterday and today was "I don't remember"?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to say so at many occasions, and again, I would like to say that this is a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I put it to you that when testifying about these events, when speaking off the top of your head, you cannot remember most of what you testified about before this Tribunal unless you consult your notes. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not totally. I think that I can remember very much also without using my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, that was evidently not the case yesterday, because when I told you not to use your notes, most of your replies were to the effect that you didn't remember. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, often I had to give that answer, because I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lars.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination. I wish to move the witness statement of witness Lars Brolund, dated -- to be entered into evidence. I also move to have the notes the witness used tendered into evidence. And I have an objection. I wish to draw the Chamber's attention to this issue, Exhibit P23, the protest note of General Strugar sent on that day. I draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the fact that the original in B/C/S does not correspond to the translation into English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll take those in order, Mr. Rodic. But may I call on you, Ms. Somers, with respect to the desire firstly to tender the statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, most of the -- many of the Chambers of the Tribunal have taken the view that the sole use of a witness statement, except for a witness statement of the accused, pursuant to Rule 63, would be only for the purpose of impeachment at trial and not submitted as evidence. A skilled examiner would use the statement to ask questions from -- for purposes of cross-examination, but the statement itself should not normally, at least in this Tribunal, go into evidence. If there is another practice, and I'm aware that apparently during Mr. Stringer's testimony, there was -- the statement was moved in, but it is unusual, except, again, either as a Rule 63 or if it's a Rule 92 bis or under the -- I think it's 87, the new use of a statement, in lieu of complete direct. But I see no real reason, under the Rules or in the examination in this case, to so admit. I think that there has been an ample opportunity to make reference to both notes and statement, and I'm simply concerned about a practice that may develop a life of its own which has not been the practice here and in most -- I cannot speak to all jurisdictions, but certainly here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I understand it, the desire of Mr. Rodic is to be able to refer to the original statement, to be able to contrast it with the evidence that was actually given, in particular, the number of matters to which the witness now was unable to personally recollect, and I think I would anticipate that Mr. Rodic would want to point out the extent of the statement, which is now not in the personal recollection of Mr. Brolund. I would anticipate, in support of submissions that the Tribunal -- the Chamber should attach less weight to the evidence of Mr. Brolund and should approach his evidence with care, because of the extent to which he is now unable to remember details from 12 or 13 years ago. And as I would understand it, it's for that reason that Mr. Rodic desires to have the actual statement before us, so that we can appreciate the extent of the divergence between what may have been the recollection of the witness some time ago and what is now the actual recollection. Approached on that basis, it certainly is, in my experience, a proper evidentiary process to tender the past statement. It's not that the statement becomes evidence of matters which have not now been confirmed by Mr. Brolund as being matters which he can confirm and speak about of his own recollection, because he has expressly indicated as to much of it that he cannot now recollect that aspect. That being so, it doesn't seem to me that it can disadvantage your position if the statement goes in, but it may be able to be put to the source of use that I've anticipated Mr. Rodic would want to put it to at some future time. Is it your submission, Ms. Somers, that there is something in the Rules against that or that there is an established practice against that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Rules, I believe, Your Honour, do not address it. The only actual, specific indication in the Rules, other than Rule 92 bis - and I might miss some other similar exceptional practices - would be the caution in a Rule 63, where it says what you say may be used in evidence, period. So that type of statement, it is anticipated that the statement of an accused, or potentially the statement of a witness under Rule 42, might also be contemplated directly. But generally speaking, example would have been the use of statements in the case of Kvocka. They were used exclusively for impeachment purposes, with a requirement that the cross-examination be dealt with point by point from the statement, entered into the record. It becomes more helpful, I think, for us to know what the practice will be in the absence of any truly addressed Rule, but I think if one were to comb through the jurisprudence or just to look at the practice, because it may not reflect itself in true jurisprudence; it would just be Court records - it is the exception -- there have been instances, I'm aware, where by agreement of the parties there have been statements admitted, and perhaps serving as direct before the institution of the recent Rule change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I make the point that what is being asked here is that the statement of a Prosecution witness be tendered, not the statement of a witness called by the Defence. So it's not an attempt to use the statement for self-serving purposes. And it is being put in merely as the foundation for submissions going to credit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. It has -- in the cases in which I have cited you, for example, Kvocka, when there was perhaps a wish by the Prosecution to put a Defence statement in, it appeared that it was again viewed as not the proper subject of a -- of admission. In this instance, I think the witness has been very clear about, and honest, about the need to rely on notes. The witness has indicated that what was said in his statement two years ago was his own, not coached in any way. And the fact that he has indicated that much of it is related to time is not unusual. Police officers who have hundreds of reports from 20 years ago will have no independent recollection of a particular incident, irrespective of how important it may be to the Court, to the witness, to the victim, or to the victim. So if there's -- I wanted to make sure that the Chamber understood that this is how the Prosecution has been effectively told it was in the course of the years, and if there is a reason that the Chamber sees my position as meriting overruling, I certainly wanted to make the record on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that. There is generally reason for reluctance about the tendering of the statements of witnesses unless there is good reason for it, and in this case, frankly, I'm inclined to agree with you that it's borderline, that even for the purposes of credibility, that it is necessary to tender it, because Mr. Rodic has been so careful in going through the passages that he now -- that the witness has now made clear he does not presently remember. But it would seem to me, for the reasons that I've indicated, and because the witness's notes made at the time are there, and therefore, there is value for the purposes of assessing credibility in comparing his notes at the time with the written statement that he made to your offices of the Prosecution some two years ago. I think on this occasion there is justification for receiving into evidence the statement of the witness, so that it will be received, and in a moment we'll be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Rodic, already in evidence as P21 are the notes, or at least a copy of the notes made by the witness, with translation. I think that's sufficient for your purposes, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. Let me just add briefly to what Your Honour has said. I fully agree with everything Your Honour has stated. I only wish to add that admitting statements into evidence is nothing new before the Tribunal, apart from the case of Kvocka, which was raised by my learned friend. I worked on that case, and I know that statements were admitted in the same manner. The same goes for the Keraterm case and I'm sure for many other cases that were heard before this Tribunal, where witness statements were tendered with the same purpose. Of course, they are used to check the witness's credibility. With respect to this particular witness, although Your Honour states that we received a copy of his notes, marked as Exhibit P21, we also feel that the copy, where parts have been highlighted, which the witness has before him, should be moved into evidence, because there is evidently a great difference in the replies of the witness during the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination. Both examinations refer to the time period covered by the indictment, and also during the examination-in-chief, the witness made his replies consulting his notes and reading from his notes. Most of the replies he gave were read out from the highlighted part of his notes. I assert that important matters in these notes have been skipped over, that he has not responded to important questions relating to these notes, which were put in cross-examination, and that there is a great difference between P21 and the statement made in 2002, which should also be based on these notes, and what the witness said before the Tribunal yesterday and today, consulting the highlighted notes he has before him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. I hadn't appreciated that what you were referring to was the set of notes actually in the hands of the witness at the present time. But I'm inclined to suggest, without even calling on Ms. Somers, that you have answered your own proposition, as you have pointed out you will want to submit that there are differences between the three different versions. We don't need the highlighted notes to know what the witness gave in evidence here. We have the transcript. So the highlighted notes really are not going to help us one way or the other. What will be important, if you persist in this submission when the time comes, will be for us to compare what the witness's original notes at the time were, what his statement was, and what his evidence in Court has been. So really, I can suggest to you that I think there would be no value at all in receiving into evidence the copy which the witness marked up as he was preparing to give his evidence. You've got all that you need there in the present material. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see Ms. Somers on her feet. Are you wanting to submit something more about that, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. No, Your Honour. You saved me a lot of energy there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I'm jumping in, but when I see something to be clear I'm going ahead with it. Now the third matter to be raised was the question of some difference between the original version and the English language version, and I was going to ask Mr. Rodic to indicate what he sees to be the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I first explain something to the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That the translation attached is the document received by the Croatians. This is not a translation done by this institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have that in evidence already.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: They came in together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So if it's a question of simply requiring an additional official translation that is certainly not difficult to do, but this is what actually came in to the parties who received it, so it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It seems to have been translated from the evidence. It was translated on the day when it was received by somebody. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rodic, is that the issue you're concerned with or was there some other problem with the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm aware that the page in English was not done at the Tribunal, that is, that the English text is not a result of an official Tribunal translation. I simply wanted to draw the Chamber's attention to the fact that there is something that was not translated, that is in the original document and that is important. The Defence will refer to this later on. I believe that there must be a more legible copy of the document than the one we have in B/C/S. You can see the Dubrovnik fax numbers at the top of the page, showing that the fax was operational at the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Members of the Chamber had noted the fax heading, showing the 1st of December, 1991, and a name, Centar, as well as the numbers. Is that the matter that you felt had not been translated?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from this, you will see that in the English translation, it says "from JNA Boka," whereas in the original it doesn't say "JNA Boka." It says "orgram" [phoen]. It could be a telegram or a radiogram, from VPS Boka, the JNA Boka and the VPS Boka are two different things. Furthermore, it says that it is addressed to the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff. This is missing in the English version. It says for the minister, Davorin Rudolf. That's what it says in the Serbian version. This document, as can be seen from the copy, also has a reference at the bottom of the page which is not clear in the B/C/S version, but I assume that there are indications here where and when this was sent, by whom, who received it, at what time, and so on. So that an official translation by CLSS of this B/C/S document would be useful, in addition to the English translation that is already appended to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jokic. I think, as Ms. Somers -- Mr. Rodic. I beg your pardon. As Ms. Somers has already indicated, she will be happy to arrange for a translation of the document, as far as it is legible. There would appear, however, to be some question about the legibility of some three lines or four lines, if they're part of the document, toward the foot of the document. And perhaps that can be looked into in due course, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It certainly can, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Well, that having been accomplished, we now turn to your re-examination, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just a couple of points, if I may, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Brolund, you used the initials JRM in the course of your testimony. Do you recall that, JRM?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you please explain what those initials stand for?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those initials are standing for Jugoslovenska Ratna Mornarica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which means?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslavian navy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Naval force. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naval forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just from everything that's been said over the past day and such, is it -- does it appear that most of the context that you, as a monitor, had with the Croatian side were with the crisis staff or with the civilian side? Would that be -- does that seem to be a fair assessment from notes and from everything that was said in Court?

utterances.speaker: LARS JENSEN BROLUND [Resumed]
utterances.text: So in this case, it's probably so concerning Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Mr. Brolund, I'm happy to be able to tell you that that concludes the evidence that you are asked to give before the Tribunal. May we thank you for your attendance and assistance, and you're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have to find out if the next witness has actually been brought over yet. He was on standby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Might it be convenient for us to break a little earlier than usual to allow you time to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd be grateful, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would 20 minutes be long enough or would you like a little longer?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think at this time if we could start with 20 minutes and if it appears at any time there's an unforeseen delay -- is that -- let us stay with 20 minutes, and if that's okay with you, and we'll notify you of any difficulty. There should be none.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of what we talked about yesterday, and our client has made complaints about being tired, so we could just add another ten minutes to the break, to have a full half hour, so that Mr. Strugar too can get some rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think there may be some justification for that, Ms. Somers, and it will enable you to be sure of your position. So we'll adjourn for half an hour now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Prosecution's next witness, Your Honour, is Mr. Nikola Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may take a moment to introduce to the Chamber Mr. Michael Hehn, a member of our staff from the leadership research team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could I ask you to make the affirmation, if the card could be handed to you. Remain seated, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you state, please, your complete name.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: My name is Nikola Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And Mr. Samardzic, your date of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 24th of October, 1935.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where were you born, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: In Ledenice, Kotor municipality in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And your nationality?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I am Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, I note you mentioned the-- I believe you said the Kotor area of Montenegro. Is that an area that is also known as, for example, Boka Kotorska, or the area containing Boka Kotorska?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Kotor is the main town in Boka Kotorska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And is that town, or that area, near to Dubrovnik, in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Boka Kotorska is an area that borders on Dubrovnik territory. The distance between the centre of Dubrovnik and Kotor itself is perhaps 70 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, your occupation during the time period February 1991 through the end of 1991, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: In 1991, my official position was general director of the Jugooceanija shipping company. At the same time, as of February of the same year, I was minister of foreign affairs for Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For how long did you continue to be minister of foreign affairs for Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I stayed in that position for exactly a year and a half. Officially, for practical purposes, I worked a little less. I left my position. I assumed my position on the 16th of February, 1991, and stayed in the position until the 13th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the interests of time, if I can just ask you if I have correctly stated the following: You have a law degree from Ljubljana University; is that correct, specialising in business law?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I obtained my degree at the law faculty in Ljubljana, via correspondence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: It was the department for economics.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. And further, you have a degree from the marine superior school in Rijeka, Croatia, with a certification as sea master. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. That superior marine school, it's a higher school, higher maritime school, in Rijeka. In addition to finishing that school, I took an exam to become a sea master.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In 1961, where did you have employment?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: In 1961, I was employed by the Jugolinija shipping company, based in Rijeka. In the same year, I obtained my degree at the higher maritime school. It was in the same year that I took an exam to become sea master.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In 1964, you returned to your native region of Boka - I'm sorry - of Kotor in Montenegro, and what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: In 1964, I was promoted and became sea captain. I had been second mate for Jugolinija up to that point, and from then on I was the commander of the ship. For Jugooceanija, until 1971.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In 1970, you went to Geneva to attend a United Nations conference, an organisation abbreviated as UNCDAT. Would you please tell us what the conference was about and what that particular organisation is.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: This was a specialisation course for maritime management and economy, organised by the United Nations, United Nations Conference on Development and Trade. I attended and took part in this specialisation course, which lasted six months, following which I attended practical courses in Oslo, in Norway, with the Leif Hoegh company. I had been admitted there based on an admission exam that I had passed in Belgrade. I was selected and I spent nine months there working with the UN.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In 1971, you were promoted within the ranks of Jugooceanija, in Kotor. To what position were you promoted, or what position did you then hold?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: After completing my specialisation courses in Geneva and Oslo, I started working in Kotor at Jugooceanija's head office. I was an administrator at first and then I became port captain, which means that I monitored our ships around the ports of the world, Jugooceanija's ships, and I became nautical inspector following that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you at the time a member of the League of Communists, or the Communist Party of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In 1974, did you enter into the Yugoslav parliament as a member? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. If so, can you describe where that parliament met.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The system was self-management. The party system was no longer in place in Yugoslavia, and I had been elected to the assembly of Yugoslavia. The first deputy assembly. I was not gainfully employed there. I would go there two or three times a month to attend sessions in Belgrade, depending on what sort of sessions they were, plenary or just some of the boards.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In 1978, you were appointed president of the Association for Self-management for Foreign Trade in Montenegro, a post which you held until 1982. What were your principal duties there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: In this position, I had to distribute foreign currency, that is, hard currency, to companies in Montenegro. At that time, the duty was also to cooperate in terms of the exchange of hard and foreign currency with other companies throughout Yugoslavia. This was a time of incipient crisis and hard currency was running out. So that's why self-managing interest communities for relations with foreign countries were set up for the first time. This was a difficult position, because we did not have enough hard currency and foreign currency, and yet, at the same time, we had to secure imports, raw materials, and everything that Montenegro's industry needed to survive.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In 1983, you became the representative of the Yugoslav chamber of commerce in Sydney, Australia. How long did you remain in that position, and were you still at the time in some way affiliated with your company Jugooceanija?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: According to the system that was in place in Yugoslavia at the time, my employment with Jugooceanija was dormant for the period. I became an employee of Yugoslavia's chamber of commerce, and I became their representative based in Sydney for Australia and New Zealand. Following the completion of my term there, a five-year term, because I had spent a year in Brisbane as the director of Yugoslavia's pavilion at the World Expo, after that I returned to Jugooceanija.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you, when you returned to Jugooceanija, do you mean that you returned to Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I returned on New Year's Eve, 1989, following the completion of my duties in Brisbane, once the Expo 88 had finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think if it were five years, perhaps you can correct me, New Year's Eve of 1988, is that correct, December 31st of 1988?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I apologise. I may have made a mistake. New Year's Eve, I mean the end of 1988. That's when I left Australia and returned to Montenegro with my family. That was the beginning of 1989, the time when I returned to my country. I had spent a full five years in Australia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Upon your return to Montenegro, what changes, if any, had you observed in the government taking place shortly after that return?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of January, 1989, there occurred the so-called anti-bureaucratic revolution in Montenegro. Young people came to power and the old leaders had been removed following large rallies and unrest from the people of Montenegro. People came out into the streets to show their discontent, especially so in Titograd, which was the capital at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And which -- if you can name some of the young leaders to whom you referred, it would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: There were several. The leaders were Momir Bulatovic, and Milo Djukanovic, who were, to all practical intents, the leaders of the revolution. I will use the term "revolution" even if this was not a proper revolution. However, they were the leaders of the movement which led to change in Montenegro at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You mentioned Momir Bulatovic. Did Mr. Bulatovic hold a role in the government of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Not up to that point. He did not have any official position. He was a teaching assistant at a university, and suddenly he entered politics and became a leader in Montenegro. Then there were the elections, and he has been an active politician and official ever since, that is, up to two years ago, when his term of office with Yugoslavia's government ended.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What role did he hold? What position did he hold as an active politician?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: In the early days, he had been elected president of the presidency of the Republic of Montenegro. This was pursuant to the old system that was in place, where you had four other members of the presidency, and he was the chairman, the president.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In October of 1991, what position -- what political position did Mr. Momir Bulatovic hold?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: In October of 1991, he was the president of the presidency of the Republic of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You mentioned also an individual named Djukanovic. Did there come a point where Mr. Djukanovic became a political figure in Montenegro, and if so, what position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: He also came along and reached the top, following the anti-bureaucratic revolution, of course, he was not elected vice-president of the government the same day, but rather, after the elections in Montenegro, he was appointed to the first government that followed the change. As far as I remember, the government was set up on the 16th of February, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In October of 1991, can you tell us, please, what position Mr. Djukanovic held.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: He was the president of Montenegro's government, or rather, prime minister. We refer to the position as the president of the government of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Going back for just a moment to your other work. In November of 1989, you were elected to be a member of the Montenegrin parliament. Where did the Montenegrin parliament convene?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The Montenegrin parliament convened in Titograd, the capital. The name is now Podgorica, but back then it was still Titograd, since 1948, and was renamed Podgorica. So the parliament, or rather, the sessions of the Montenegrin parliament were always in Podgorica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In 1990, in July, you were elected as a representative of Montenegro to the federal Chamber of Republics. What type of duties did you have, and where did you carry out any meetings or duties?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: This was a vestige of the deputy system in the assemblies, and Montenegro, as all other republics, was supposed to appoint 20 deputies to the council of the republics, which was part of the Yugoslav assembly. The elections were held at the Montenegrin assembly, because it was up to the assembly to appoint its candidates. There was a secret vote and I was elected. Although I had not been previously nominated by the authorities. It was the deputies who put forward my name, and following the vote, I became one of the 20 deputies. That's how I became a deputy to the Yugoslav Assembly, in addition to my role in the Montenegrin Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated that you held formerly the position of foreign minister of Montenegro. How did you become the foreign minister of Montenegro? Were you appointed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: No. Milo Djukanovic, who held the new -- who led the new government, asked me to accept to become foreign minister, which I resisted for a while, because I could not do both things at the same time. It was quite a burden to bear, because I was also still manager of Oceanija, Jugooceanija. After lengthy negotiations, I accepted to become -- to remain the manager of Jugooceanija and to become foreign minister. I was still officially employed by Jugooceanija. They paid my salary. Sometimes I would travel to Titograd, or rather, Podgorica, to discharge my duties as foreign minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How old was Mr. Djukanovic when he requested you to become prime minister?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: He was 28.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you play an active role in the affairs of Montenegro as its foreign minister?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I tried to play a role that was as active as possible at the time, because the situation kept changing in Montenegro on a daily basis. I tried to contribute as much as I could. Of course, I was in a position to influence certain things. I was in a position to cooperate, to the extent possible, with both Mr. Bulatovic and also Mr. Djukanovic, who was the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated earlier that the changes in government that you found upon your return from Australia to Montenegro involved a younger generation. How would you describe the level of experience of some of the other members of the government? When I say "government," I'm referring to the ministers.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I was the most senior member there. It was quite obvious to me that most of them had not had any hands-on experience. Milo Djukanovic, prime minister, that was the first place he ever worked, the first employment, that is. There were a number of ministers, other ministers, that had had precious little experience. Most of them, that is, all of them -- none of them spoke any foreign languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did you speak foreign languages, Mr. Samardzic? If so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Montenegrin, of course, is my mother tongue, in addition to which I also speak English, Italian, Russian, and Spanish.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were these skills valued skills, as a member of the government of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Certainly. It proved very useful, because I was in a position to communicate. It was much easier for me when it came to international contacts than for other members of the government, especially whenever we travelled abroad, also whenever we were meeting foreign diplomats, it was much easier for me to establish communication. Often times, an ambassador would come and visit from an area that was not English-speaking and it was possible for me to communicate in Italian or in Spanish, which means that communication was much easier for me than for the remaining members of Montenegrin government.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd like to just ask you if you could identify, briefly, the following personalities from the former Yugoslavia: Branko Kostic. Just who the person was and the role. Putting it in a time frame of the autumn of 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Branko Kostic, I must say, he comes from a very good Montenegrin family. His father and his entire family had taken part in the liberation war. He, unfortunately, became a fervent nationalist and had earned the trust of Slobodan Milosevic in Montenegro. He was elected to the Yugoslav presidency. He had replaced Nenad Bucin, when Nenad Bucin was forced to resign, and Kostic replaced him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Borisav Jovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Borisav Jovic was also an ultra nationalist who followed the policies of Slobodan Milosevic and who was also a member of the Yugoslav presidency on behalf of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Blagoje Adzic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Blagoje Adzic is a general. He was the chief of Yugoslav army's Main Staff, also a toady to Milosevic, obviously, who also played a very negative role in the break-up of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Veljko Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Veljko Kadijevic was the federal secretary, or rather, the federal minister for National Defence. He was also an important player during the break-up of Yugoslavia. In my estimate, he played a negative role, contributing to conflict and to the eventual disintegration of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you indicate the federal Ministry of Defence, is that also known as the SSNO? And what does that stand for, please?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: That stands for Federal Secretariat for National Defence. The abbreviation is used for the former Yugoslavia's defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated, Mr. Samardzic, the proximity of your home region to Dubrovnik. Had you yourself been to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was, in your estimation, there, let us say, up to the autumn, or perhaps a bit earlier, in 1991, a generally positive attitude between the people of Montenegro and those of Croatia, and specifically, the area of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The relations between population of Montenegro, especially in Boka Kotorska and the population of Dubrovnik, had been brotherly, at least before the war, in terms of the economy, in terms of culture, social and private life. There was no difference to be seen anywhere. No line of separation. We lived together and we worked together, which was especially important in terms of maritime affairs, which is the branch of economy that I belonged to. You had tourism and maritime affairs, which were the two most important branches of the local economy, and these were very much dependent on Dubrovnik's own economy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you noticed a change in the relationship between at least some of the population, and perhaps official population of Montenegro, to Dubrovnik and other parts of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everything was new for me when I returned from Australia. The situation deteriorated from day to day. Let me give you just one example. When, because of the new policy that the Montenegrin leadership was implementing in relation to Croatia, and this was before October 1991, before the outbreak of the war, the Croatian INA company stopped shipments of oil to Jugopetrol, which was the main Montenegrin supplier, and there was misunderstanding and the worsening of relations. I was given the task of going to Zagreb with another minister in order to ask the Croatian government to again allow supplies of petroleum to be sent to Montenegro. And contrary to the wishes of the then-director of INA, several Croatian ministers did their best to re-establish the supplies to Montenegro. This was just before the events of October 1991. It was in the summer, I believe it was in August 1991, when there was already discord, but we endeavoured to resolve this in the best possible manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you begin to notice any other indications of hostility towards Croatia, perhaps in the form of propaganda or hate language, hate speeches, even coming out of such bodies as the parliament?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: At the time, Montenegro organised its multiparty assembly for the first time. Some of these parliamentary parties were ultranationalist, others were in favour of an independent Montenegro. There was a great deal of tension mounting, not only between particular political parties in Montenegro, but also in relation to Croatia. It was thought that Croatia and Slovenia were separatists, that they wanted the collapse of Yugoslavia, that they were preparing to attack Montenegro, or to secede. So that from day to day, the propaganda grew and it didn't bring any good. Montenegrin television broadcast their own ideas. The Montenegrin papers and the Belgrade papers aired their views, and the tensions mounted. This was on the eve of the military conflict that broke out later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Does the day 25 June --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Does the date 25 June have any significance in your mind? 1991, of course.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: This was the day when the Croatian parliament, as far as I can remember, declared that Croatia was to secede and become an independent state. I think that was the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what about Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Slovenia did the same, at the same time. In our part of the world, we paid more attention to Croatia, because it was a neighbouring country. But Slovenia did declare independence at the same time as Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the term, and I mean no offence when I say it, "Ustasha"? If you are familiar, what does the term normally mean, and is it meant in a complimentary fashion or a derogatory fashion?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: It has an extremely derogatory meaning, a negative connotation, and this name was used to denote the independent military formations of the independent state of Croatia in World War I [as interpreted]. They committed terrible atrocities over Serbs and Croats. The word "Ustasha" meant something evil. I have to say, however, that the word, the root of the word, actually comes from an ancient word meaning "rebel," and it didn't always have the same meaning. In the 19th, there were rebels in Montenegro who referred to themselves as Ustashe, and the same goes for Herzegovina. However, during World War II, this word became compromised. It acquired a negative meaning. So that in 1991, using this word was the worst word you could possibly use, and the Montenegrin politicians used this word to refer to the entire Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, I note from the context of your response, you indicated World War II was the point that the word took on a negative meaning. I note that on page 37, line 25, you talked about the independent state of Croatia and you said World War I. Did you mean World War II?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: That was an error maybe. It was in the Second World War that the independent state of Croatia existed. There was no independent state of Croatia in world war 1. It was part of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you familiar, Mr. Samardzic, with formations, principally Montenegrin formations, called the 3rd Volunteers Brigade of the Titograd Corps and the 5th Proletariat or Proletarian Montenegrin Brigade? Have you heard of such formations?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I am aware that such formations existed. The 5th Montenegrin Brigade bore the name of a celebrated brigade from World War I [as interpreted], commanded by Savo Kovacevic, and it was based in Titograd. It was one of the most famous units in the fight against fascism in World War II. And this unit was meant to carry on these illustrious traditions. However, in 1991, they failed to do so. The Volunteers Corps was a paramilitary formation. The very word "volunteers" testified to this. I know less about this unit. I know that it did exist, and in 1991, when the war broke out, there were several such volunteers units. Some were more voluntary and others less, but they cannot be compared to the 5th Montenegrin Brigade. The 5th Brigade was an elite unit of the national liberation struggle of Yugoslavia. This was the tradition they were supposed to maintain, but unfortunately they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Before I continue --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Before I continue, I note again from the context of your complete response, you were referring to World War II with the Savo Kovacevic Brigade, and on page 38, line 25, your response was taken down as the 5th Montenegrin Brigade bore the name of a celebrated brigade from World War I, commanded by Savo Kovacevic. Was that to have read, from the context, World War II?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Savo Kovacevic was in World War II. I don't know how World War I crept in. But it was one of the most celebrated brigades of the national liberation struggle of Yugoslavia, the 4th and 5th Montenegrin Brigade and the 1st and 2nd Dalmatian Brigades were very famous brigades, illustrious brigades, mutually connected. The 5th Montenegrin and 2nd Dalmatian Brigades, under the command of Savo Kovacevic, were part of the 3rd Division, and the activities of this famous unit commanded by Savo Kovacevic are something that is unique in the history of warfare, in view of their sacrifices and the weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to please distribute two documents. They appear to be hefty, but in fact there are only several pages that I wish to make reference to. I just did not separate them. Because of the weight of it and the bulk of it, Your Honours, we will not use Sanction. I think it's more helpful just to have the hard copies. In front of everyone are documents, one bearing ERN 01899218, which is a bulletin from the 5th Proletarian or Proletariat Montenegrin Brigade, dated December 1991; and the second document, ERN 01077597, is an information bulletin from the 3rd Volunteer Brigade of the Titograd Corps, dated 27 January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, these are corps, these are formations that you have indicated you are familiar -- the existence of which you are familiar with?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. These, I see, are their internal bulletins from the war front, where the 5th Proletariat Brigade was. But this is far from the traditions of the 5th Montenegrin Brigade. Evidently --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I can just ask for a moment, please: If you could turn again to just selected pages, as the point I wish to make is perhaps indicated throughout, I will refer only to the English translation part. But if you would look, for example, in the bulletin of the 3rd Volunteers Brigade, which would be 01077597, that particular document. And look on the page which bears, at the top, the number L, as in Leo, 0096686. Looking in the first complete paragraph, and I'm just drawing your attention to a phrase. It says: "Our goal and our will to battle against the Ustashas were obvious." And then it goes on to say: "A cannon had been deployed at the crossroads. The barrels of guns had been pointed at Dubrovnik, which is right next to us." A little below: "In fact, there were traces of the former inhabitants of these dwellings, the Ustasha hordes." I next ask you to turn your attention to the page bearing L0096704. In the middle -- underneath the caption, the first paragraph, it says: "The 5th has fun on the beaches at Vrtovi Sunca." But the particular language I'm looking at is: "It was not easy to advance over" -- I'm sorry. I'll wait until you have found it. Right. "It was not easy to advance -- it was not easy to advance over soil that had been trodden by the fascist boot, poisoned by the arrows of the HDZ, Croatian Democratic Union, and inundated with hatred for the JNA and everything Yugoslav." If you turn the page to L0096705, looking at the first complete paragraph, it says: "The 5th Company also looked after refugees." Then it indicates something illegible "terrified by the Ustashas." If you would then turn the page to L0096706, the first complete paragraph under "police officers always ready for action." Roughly in the middle, it says: "Yet at one time when, the entire brigade was in a maelstrom of battle with the Croatian Ustashas..." If you would then go on to L0096709, first complete paragraph. "On arriving at Orasac, this unit immediately established good relations with the inhabitants. To tell the truth, it was not easy to crack the icy terror which the Croatian Ustashas had managed to instil in the inhabitants." I'd ask you to then look at the second document, which is another separate bulletin for the 5th Proletarian Montenegrin Brigade. And if you'd look, please, briefly, at -- at the top it says ET, E as in Edward, T as in Tom, 0189 through - this may not be terribly helpful - 9218. I'm trying to find the best identifier for you. It's a bit difficult for us, but through 01899251. And at the bottom, it says: "3 of 29." I don't know if you can see it. I think these are -- it says "3 of 29." Has it been found where it has a line dividing it where it says "Dubrovnik fell a long time ago," and above it there's text?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, is that visible? All that I'm referring to, it's in English. But it would say at the bottom "3 of 29." Perhaps I can assist you. I think you don't have an English -- yeah, there we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At the top of -- toward the top of the page, the full paragraph, quotation: "In my estimate, the 5th Proletarian Brigade's units, carrying out war tasks, have performed them impeccably and have given the greatest contribution to dispersing Ustasha formations along the Debeli Brijeg, Dubrovnik stretch." I would ask you to turn to a page which says "12 of 29" at the bottom, 12 of 29. It says: "The curse of number 11." Is that there, Mr. Usher? The first paragraph under there where it talks about Osojnik. "A real vulture's nest. Ustashas reigned there until recently." I will stop with the examples, but, Mr. Samardzic, this type of language, the repeated references to the Croatians as Ustashas, was this something that gained momentum during the time period of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: This was a time when, in Montenegro, and certainly in Serbia, the propaganda contained a lot of hysteria against the Ustashas and against the Croatian people especially during the time of the Dubrovnik operation. Everything that happened in Croatia was declared to be done by the Ustasha. As far as I know, at least in the area bordering on Montenegro, there were no Ustasha there, except perhaps for some self-organised smaller Croatian units who were trying to defend themselves, as far as they were able to. And on the stretch between Debeli Brijeg and Dubrovnik or Cavtat, there was no large-scale fighting. The largest-scale fighting took part west of Dubrovnik, where there was more resistance by the Croatian forces, but there were no Ustasha there either. What you want to know is: Yes, the propaganda in Montenegro at that time was very hysterical and it was aimed at the Croatian people. What it says here in these bulletins is no different from what was said on television or written in newspapers. It was the same vocabulary, referring to the war operations, but also beyond that. Everything that was written in those days was aimed at compromising everything that was going on in Croatia, including the defence of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask -- I would like to move these into evidence, or tender them. If I could ask, please, for numbers, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The two bulletins will be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit numbers P25 and P26.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you distinguish which is P25, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P25 bears the ERN 01899218, and P26 bears the ERN number 01077597.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking more specifically now at the events in the Dubrovnik region: Did you attend any official meetings in Montenegro on the 1st of October, 1991? When I say "official," I mean attended by officials. I don't necessarily mean officially set.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of October, I attended a meeting, but only half a meeting, because I had other business that I had to do. And this was a meeting held at the government of Montenegro. It was a meeting of the presidency, the cabinet, and the generals of Montenegro. There were several generals who participated in the meeting. I arrived halfway through the meeting and attended the second half, because Momir Bulatovic had sent me to Cetinje, to see off Mr. Wejnaendts. This was a Dutch diplomat, who was Lord Carrington's deputy, and who, on that day, had visited Montenegro to try to prevent the start of war operations. It was evening by the time I got back, and I was extremely surprised when I discovered that generals were present at a cabinet meeting in war uniforms. These were not, as far as I was able to see, camouflage uniforms, but they were the uniforms worn by generals when they are to go into action. I arrived halfway through the meeting and stayed until the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, you described the meeting as a meeting of the presidency, the cabinet, and generals of Montenegro. It appears from the level of participants, you might have had advance notice of it.
