In this case, had you had advance notice of such a meeting, given that you were a member of the cabinet, a minister?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: No. I did not receive any official invitation. I was stopped by the police at the bridge on Moraca, on my way back from the airport, where I had seen off Mr. Wejnaendts, and I was driving out of Titograd, because I lived in Kotor. I was stopped by the police, and they said, "You have to go to a cabinet meeting." I went back and I found the ministers and the presidency and the generals already conducting the meeting. And this was after I had seen off Mr. Wejnaendts at the airport, because I had spent the entire afternoon with him in Cetinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you surprised about this type of meeting and the way you came to learn of it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was shocked, because I had assured Mr. Wejnaendts there would be no war. I have to say that he had come to Titograd to see whether there was going to be a war and to try to prevent one, if there was a war in the offing. And he tried to learn from Momir Bulatovic and me whether war operations were about to start. He had been informed that on that day, the war from Dubrovnik was to begin. I was deeply convinced that the JNA would not attack Dubrovnik, and I had done my utmost to convince him that it was impossible for an attack to be launched from Montenegro on Croatia. And it was in this conviction that I had arrived at the cabinet meeting, not expecting anything like that to happen. It was already late, about 8.00 or 9.00 p.m., when I arrived, and then I saw that things were really serious.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated that when you got to this meeting, you recognised or you saw some generals. Can you indicate who among the military you observed to be there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I did not know those generals personally, but I knew who they were, from photographs and from the way they were addressed at the meeting. General Strugar was there, General Jeremic, Damjanovic, Babic, who was Montenegro's defence minister, and several other officers, who were seated around a table where ministers were usually seated, around the main table, plus a number of other people who had not earlier attended meetings of the cabinet as deputies or assistant ministers, from different ministries, especially from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as well as members of the cabinet, in addition to Momir Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm terribly sorry. You indicated -- you said General Strugar. Are you referring to General Pavle Strugar?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's the one I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And when you indicated Minister Babic, was that Bozidar Babic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Bozidar Babic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I note, Mr. Samardzic, that your statement had the name of Admiral Jokic there, and you have indicated to the Office of the Prosecutor that that was in error. Is it correct now that Admiral Jokic was not at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: There was an error. Admiral Jokic was not present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would also indicate that any other corrections to your statement have also been provided to the Defence, as indicated to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, looking at the subject under discussion at that meeting, what was being discussed? What was it that would have brought a general like Strugar to a meeting like that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: General Strugar, while I was there, he spoke, and he said that we had been attacked and that we had to defend ourselves. 30.000 Ustasha were about to attack Boka Kotorska and Montenegro had to defend itself. That's what he said. Later he also said that we would no doubt be successful in defending ourselves and that we would manage to defend with minimum losses and that the army would do everything to keep the losses down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In your statement, I want to ask you about the wording, as it -- I believe it to be significant. You said Strugar said that he was happy that the Montenegro --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe the answer is -- the question is not correct. My learned friend and colleague, I am sure, can ask Mr. Samardzic what General Strugar said. But certainly not by quoting what the statement says, and thus reminding him of what he wishes to say. Mr. Samardzic is perfectly capable of telling us what he remembers. There's no problem there. It was only the phrasing of the question which I think is inappropriate in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm happy to rephrase, Your Honour. I'm happy to rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. I think in an area so critical you should avoid --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm happy to rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was General Strugar's attitude about the Montenegrins fighting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: General Strugar said that we had been attacked, that 30.000 Ustashas were about to attack Boka, or Montenegro, that we would defend ourselves and thereby defend Yugoslavia. He said that the losses would be kept down to an absolute minimum and that we should take all measures to defend our country. It wasn't only General Strugar who spoke along these lines, but rather also Momir Bulatovic, and they enjoyed the support of all the other members of the cabinet, that is, the ministers. Everyone spoke. Even I spoke at the meeting, saying: If we have been attacked, we shall defend ourselves." General Strugar's reputation was great, and I was convinced that he had a point there, that we had indeed been attacked. All my colleagues were unanimous in their desire to defend the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not General Strugar referred to the Croatians as Croatians, or by some other term?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, again, the phrasing of the question is inappropriate. My apologies. The question can be: How General Strugar referred to the Croats, but not suggest anything in the phrasing of the question itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said before, he called the Croatian units Ustashas. He said 30.000 Ustashas were about to attack Boka Kotorska. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Had you been aware of any impending attack? Had you heard any such thing actually happening before coming to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had heard this from Hrvoje Kacic, first and foremost, who was a Croatian official and a friend from my youth. In The Hague, when we met 15 days earlier, he told me that the army was preparing an attack on Croatia. I did my best to convince him that there would be no such attack by the JNA. That's what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, perhaps -- I'm sorry to interrupt you. Perhaps my question was less than clear. I was referring to: Had you heard of any attack on Boka or on Montenegro by the Croatian forces occurring before you walked into that meeting, or any credible threat of an attack?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: That evening, a document was distributed to everyone that I think was drafted by Jovanovic, who was the security chief in Herceg-Novi, to the effect that Croats were causing incidents near the border. However, in my opinion, nothing really important was said on that evening. There must have been some sort of misunderstanding, or rather, there was a report, but the report did not indicate any threat of war. There was nothing for me to see on the Croatian part, an attack on Montenegro in the offing, or anything like that, or, for that matter, what General Strugar was talking about, that all of a sudden 30.000 Ustashas would be about to launch an attack on Crno Gora, Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was that the first you had heard of these 30.000 Ustasha suggestion? Was that the first time you had heard of it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The first time I heard about that, from Momir Bulatovic also, because he also spoke that same evening and spoke about the 30.000 Ustasha and how we were supposed to defend our country. He said this two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At that time, do you know what role General Strugar held in Montenegro? Are you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I did know, although I did not keep track of General Strugar's exact position at the time. He was the commander of the Territorial Defence of Montenegro, and the commander of the 2nd Operations Group of the JNA. That's what it was called then, which covered not only Montenegro but also a section of Herzegovina and perhaps even of Serbian territory. I'm not sure what exactly it covered, the 2nd Operations Group. But certainly, General Strugar was one of the top military commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At the time, had you ever heard of a person named Ruzinovski?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ruzinovski, Luzinovski... I did hear that there was a general of that name, a Macedonian, who was the commander of the 2nd Operations Group for General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have any sense of whether or not, from anything that was said or done at that meeting, whether or not General Strugar would occupy any type of role in what came to be known as the Dubrovnik campaign?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: By all means, General Strugar was the commander of the forces that attacked Dubrovnik. Later that evening, it was clear. I had been surprised at first, but then the meeting was over and it became perfectly clear that there would be a campaign to conquer Dubrovnik and its territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You said a few moments ago that General Strugar, when he spoke, spoke about, I believe the term you used was liberating Dubrovnik at a minimum cost. Now, was that representation by the general who was commander of the Territorial Defence, as you say, was that made in the presence --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. Can my learned friend and colleague please indicate where, in which line of the statement exactly, he stated this. She is trying to insinuate bits and pieces from the statement, which, with your permission, we have succeeded in preventing. And again, she is insinuating and suggesting certain kinds of wording to the witness. Where exactly did Mr. Samardzic state this throughout his testimony? What you're referring to now, where exactly has this been stated?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I cannot refer to page and line, but my recollection was minimum cost, and I believe I recollect hearing that phrase. If there's any doubt about the use of the phrase, I will simply, with Your Honours' permission, rephrase the question to that of which I am absolutely certain, which is the term "Dubrovnik" and "minimum cost."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is that familiar to you? Is that what you had said earlier, Mr. Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you speak, Mr. Petrovic, I may have missed it, but I was not aware of that phrase having been used by the witness in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I thought -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. I thought I heard it. I recall "minimum cost" and I thought that it was said. If it was not, then I request that that be stricken and I refer to the term "minimum cost," which I know I did hear from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're checking back in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm informed it may be losses, Your Honour, not cost. Perhaps the word "losses." Page 23, line 23. 23, 23. If I am incorrect in my phrasing, I would ask to simply withdraw it and correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It appears there, in a passage that you spoke, rather than the witness, it was in a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry. The reference was above. I have to search the record for it. But I can simply avoid that by coming back with a more direct question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I should hear Mr. Petrovic, who has been waiting patiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the first problem we have is Mr. Samardzic is listening to our discussion, and this in itself may affect his further testimony. Secondly, my learned friend and colleague, Ms. Somers, due to a lack of caution, deliberately or not, used precisely the terms to which we had just objected, whereby we effectively prevented her from using those terms. They are not in the document which in front of her. In this way, Ms. Somers is trying to directly influence the testimony of Mr. Samardzic by suggesting to him potential wordings, while Mr. Samardzic needs no assistance from anyone. He's perfectly able to testify without anyone's assistance. The way in which Ms. Somers is conducting this examination-in-chief may affect our client's interests. Therefore, may the Chamber please caution Ms. Somers about the wording of her questions to Mr. Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I let the Chamber know that the passage to which I was referring is found on page 23, lines 18 through 24, and I assure the Chamber that the Prosecution is not trying to direct. I agree with Mr. Petrovic; this witness is more than able to answer everything for himself. And if I may read back the answer, I will then proceed on the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just pause a moment while we find the passage. Did you say page 23, line 18?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. My colleague, Ms. McCreath, has shown me on the laptop it shows 23, line 18, starting with the phrase "General Strugar."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We haven't found it yet, I'm sorry to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Unless there's different pagination. It would be roughly, Your Honours, after Mr. Samardzic indicating that Admiral Jokic was not present at that meeting, several lines after that, if that would help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have a time reference?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. 16:59, if the laptop is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I can be of assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have found a reference at page -- bottom of page 46 and over on to page 47. "General Strugar spoke. He said that we had been attacked and we had to defend ourselves. 30.000 Ustasha were about to attack Boka Kotorska and Montenegro had to defend itself. Later he said that: We would no doubt be successful in defending ourselves and we would manage to defend with minimum losses and that the army would do everything to keep the losses down." That would appear to be the passage to which you were referring, Ms. Somers. It contains no reference to the town Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My error, Your Honour. I thought that it had been there. And since it is now read back, I will withdraw the last question, as it answers the previous two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, and I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, I think there is some substance in the concern of Mr. Petrovic. In two or three matters now of some critical concern, in your eagerness to move on quickly, you have been leading on matters that are material, and I think it would be appropriate for you to be much more cautious about that, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I certainly will. I am mindful of the time, and I am moving a little perhaps too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, on matters as important as this, I think you'll appreciate that Mr. Petrovic is well and properly concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. If I can just take a look at the last question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At this particular meeting on the 1st of October, Mr. Samardzic, was a commitment, in your opinion, made by General Strugar as to the course of the campaign?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Of course, he expressed his commitment that the campaign should take place, that the country should be defended and, and that the Croatian attack should be stopped, or rather, the Ustasha attack, as he called them, their attack on Boka Kotorska and on Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- with your permission. Again in this question we have an implication, an insinuation, something that Mr. Samardzic is not saying. He's talking about a campaign, and Mr. Samardzic says yes, he expressed his commitment, commitment to defence from this attack. He's not referring to any campaign. You can check the time reference, 17:15, page 54. There is no reference whatsoever to any campaign, Ms. Somers. It's you who keeps referring to a campaign, not Mr. Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, does the term, military term, and we are now talking military action. It is a term which I would use in the normal course of speech. If there is a problem with the term, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is a term capable of both an aggressive and defensive connotation. Mr. Petrovic is hearing it as an aggressive. You seem to be viewing it as a defensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is in the context of the allegation of 30.000 troops, and this is the context in which I am addressing "campaign."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we're now found on page 50, the last answer on the page of the witness, that he mentioned that "the meeting was over and it became perfectly clear that there would be a campaign to conquer Dubrovnik and its territory," which is an aggressive reference, as I would read it. So that it is that that you were taking up on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honours, it is both, because of the nature of the discussion and of what has just been discussed as about to -- Mr. Samardzic indicated, about to be undertaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have we disrupted events enough for me to suggest that this might be a convenient time for a break? And you can collect your thoughts, then, Ms. Somers, and with some luck, it will not be necessary for Mr. Petrovic or ourselves to interrupt you when we resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think that will be a great idea. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll break, then, for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Excuse me. I just want to check. Thank you very much. I'm sorry. I had to check a reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, after this meeting that you've described -- actually, excuse me. I'll return to the meeting for a moment. Can you approximate the number of persons who were attending the meeting, the number of attendees? Are you not --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you approximate the number of persons attending the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't count them. I wasn't able to. But I'm sure that there were more than 25 all together, if not 30. The room was full. There's a long table there, and during normal sessions, when the generals and the members of the presidency were not there, during normal cabinet meetings, there were always empty seats around that table, and on that occasion, the room was absolutely full.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you happen to observe anyone either recording or taking any notes, if you observed it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Minutes were kept, and the meeting was recorded. Cabinet sessions were recorded regularly, and minutes were kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At any meetings subsequent to this meeting, was there ever any further discussion about 30.000 Ustashe?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: No. It was obvious on the next day that no Ustasha had attacked Montenegro or Boka, but that rather our units had penetrated the territory of Croatia, of Dubrovnik. This was clear that same evening, on television, and on the following day it was completely clear. You could see from the images on television that this was all happening in the Dubrovnik area and not the area of Boka Kotorska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there any discussion at this meeting about -- well, excuse me. Let me back up. You have said, if I understood correctly, that it became clear that it was all happening in the Dubrovnik area and not in the area of Boka Kotorska. What and when happened? What happened, and when did it happen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The television reports on the same evening made it clear that, as far as the border was concerned, if any fighting was taking place, it was on Croatian territory. As I have already said, the real fighting was more to the west of Dubrovnik, and there was far less resistance on the border towards Montenegro, that is, Debeli Brijeg and Konavle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At that particular meeting, do you recall any discussion about events taking place in Croatia that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: No, not on that day. That evening, if you're referring to that evening, there was no discussion of operations in Croatia, but rather how we should defend ourselves and how we should break up the Croatian army, or the Ustasha army, as Momir Bulatovic and the generals were claiming, that the Ustashe were attacking us. Certainly, the situation was clearer on the following days, and the days that followed, but on that evening, that was when the war operation began, during this session of the cabinet and the presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say "war operations," can you be specific? What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: When I say "war operation," I mean an infantry attack, a tank and artillery attack, and everything that goes with this. Obviously, this started from Montenegro against Croatia. On that evening, we saw on television that a real war had broken out. We could only see this on television, of course. So there was a war, and that's what was said that evening, that war had started.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any commitments as to resources that were made -- or were any commitments to resources made by any of the ministers present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: That evening, what was said was that the government of Montenegro, the Ministry of the Interior, and so on, should have special police units, special organs, which would be active on the border towards Croatia and that mobilisation should be carried out. Mobilisation was to be carried out by the JNA and the government supported it, of course. The Ministry of the Interior would put the Territorial Defence and the special police units at the disposal of the army, to help them in their operations on the border with Croatia. This was discussed that evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to distribute two documents, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, before you are two documents. One should be appearing on your screen, if it is set on "computer evidence." The two documents bear ERNs B/C/S 01088616 and 01062686. I will ask you about each document, but first: Looking at the one that ends in 8616, bearing a date of 1 October -- do you see the one with 8616 at the top, the last four digits, 8616?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is this document familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I saw it when I testified against Slobodan Milosevic last time, and also I saw it in our papers, the paper Monitor published it on several occasions. I didn't see it that night on the 1st of October. It must have been drawn up after the end of the session. But it's evidently a result of the conclusions reached at that session of the 1st of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The content of the document, is the content, the material described in it, familiar to you, where the document is Presidency of the Republic of Montenegro, dated 1 October 1991, order, it has four points, and it bears the endorsement of Momir Bulatovic, president of the presidency, the first point being -- I'm sorry. Are you familiar with the content of the document in front of you? Is it familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'm fully familiar with its content. That night, these points were discussed, and the conclusions stated here were reached. This was obviously signed by the president of the presidency, Momir Bulatovic, after the end of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This particular document, which is labelled "order," has as its first point, on 2 October 1991, between 1500 and 1700 hours, referring in the head paragraph about a decision on the use of police for combat tasks of the armed forces and the use of Territorial Defence units for keeping public order and carrying out other tasks of social protection, "I hereby," indicating Bulatovic, "order, on 2 October," and I continue reading: "Carry out a mobilisation of a special police unit, the strength of a reinforced infantry company, tasked with carrying out combat operations of the armed forces in the conflict of war on the border of the Republic of Montenegro and the Republic of Croatia." 2: "Together with units of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence, the unit will perform specific military and police tasks in accordance with the mission plan, to be devised by the operative command on the Dubrovnik front." 3: "Senior police officer appointed by the minister of the interior will have the direct command of the unit." 4: "Ministry of the Interior will equip the unit with the necessary weapons, medical and quartermaster's provisions, other material and technical equipment, and will transport the units from the mobilisation location to the place needed." Is the content matter, in its entirety, familiar?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's fully familiar to me. This was decided on that night, and it was later put on this piece of paper, which was signed by Momir Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I ask you to turn your attention to the second document, the last numbers of which are 2686, dated also 1 October 1991, bearing an endorsement by Minister Pavle Bulatovic, reciting: "Pursuant to Article 3 of the order by the president of the presidency of the Republic of Montenegro and reciting a number of 01-14 of 1 October 1991, I hereby order: 1: Between 1500 and 1700 hours on 2 October 1991, mobilise a reinforced infantry detachment, strong police unit, whose task it will be to carry out combat of the armed forces in the war on the border of the Republic of Montenegro and Croatia. 2: Reinforce the unit by members of the special platoon of the special unit, and by policemen of the Titograd security centre, Niksic security centre, and Bar security centre. 3: The unit shall be under the immediate command of the assistant minister for the public security service and ministry officers appointed by him. 4: After its establishment, supply the unit with the necessary infantry weapons, and with quartermaster medical, technical, supplies and other materiel, reinforce it with two M-86 police combat vehicles and 82 millimetre mortar squad and organise the unit's transport from the mobilisation assembly point to the place of its employment. 4 -- 5: The unit shall carry out military police type combat assignments according to the employment plan, to be issued by the operative command of the Dubrovnik theatre of war." Again bearing endorsement of Pavle Bulatovic. Are you familiar with the content of this document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I didn't see that document then. I only saw it later on. It was signed by Pavle Bulatovic, the late Pavle Bulatovic. He's now deceased. He was then the minister of the interior of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The order -- the first one you looked at of Momir Bulatovic bears -- can you indicate what number is at the top, the very first order, where it says "strictly confidential, number..." The very top, on the left upper corner.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Left, 0114, strictly confidential. Titograd, the 1st of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And the second document, which refers -- the second document of Pavle Bulatovic, which refers to a number --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Strictly confidential, number 0114/2, Titograd, the 1st of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And in the centre of it, where it says "pursuant to Article 3 of the order of the president," it cites a number, strictly confidential number, in the middle of the -- above the word "order," what number is that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: In the first document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the order of Pavle Bulatovic, in the second one.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. "Pursuant to Article 3 of the order by the president of the presidency of the Republic of Montenegro, strictly confidential, number 0114, 1st of October, 1991. I hereby order ...." So he's repeating the number from the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask to tender these into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P27, document bearing ERN number 01088616; and P28, document bearing ERN number 01062686.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, there is mention of weaponry in these orders. Do you know, from any of your meetings or contacts during this time period, what, if any, weaponry may have been used in the action in Dubrovnik? If you know.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I can't see this from this document. It doesn't say that. But in that period, what was used were both light and heavy weapons. You could see that from the television reports and from the soldiers moving about Boka Kotorska. Tanks, artillery, all of that was moving in the direction of Dubrovnik. Practically all the kinds of weapons that are used in war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection about the time frame, or if a time frame was mentioned by General Strugar when he spoke about -- when he spoke at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: He didn't say exactly how many days this would last, but he did say that we would break them up very quickly. There was quite a lot of discussion about how all this would end, because, to refer back to what we discussed a while ago, they were not talking about defence only but about liberation, liberation of the territory. That was the expression used by General Strugar. And the other participants in the discussion said that the borders would be expanded; others spoke of liberation. However, there was no specific mention as to how far they would go, but they did say that the Ustashe would be broken up very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You've mentioned the term "liberation." What was your understanding of that term?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I understood that they would occupy that territory. They spoke of liberation of the territory. They said that the Ustasha were going in the direction of Boka but that we would very soon rout them. This was a discussion late at night. There were different tones that were used by the various participants in the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know if the forces that fought in Dubrovnik for the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, incurred any losses, casualties?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were casualties right away, not on the border at Debeli Brijeg, as was expected initially, but more on the west side of Dubrovnik. There were significant losses. At least, that's what they said on television. A hundred and fifty-seven men from Montenegro were killed in operations around Dubrovnik, as far as I know. Many think that the number is higher, but the official information is that 157 of them fell in the attack on Dubrovnik. I am talking of losses by the JNA. So they were not only from Montenegro, but also from Herzegovina and others who were conscripts in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the reaction in Montenegro to these losses, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Well, it was very difficult. The people did not expect there to be any losses, because promises were made that the entire operation would be completed with minimum losses. So that when the names of those who had been killed were read out on television, people were extremely upset, and resistance emerged among the people. Protest meetings were held, especially in the area of Cetinje. People sang a song, "Salovce navila klice prostinam Dubrovnice," [phoen] asking Dubrovnik to forgive them. People were indignant, in spite of the hysterical propaganda which tried to prove that we had to fight in order to conquer the Ustasha. As the days passed, it became quite evident that the campaign was leading to no good.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you learn of any actions taken against the Old Town of Dubrovnik by JNA force? Did those -- did any actions come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very soon, shelling on Dubrovnik started, and there were reports about this on television. But claims were made that the Croats were setting car tyres alight in Dubrovnik, and that is where the smoke came from. They were saying that the army was not shelling Dubrovnik, but it was clear to everyone that Dubrovnik was being shelled and that buildings were being targeted which were in the Old Town, the historical part of Dubrovnik. And this was very upsetting for people in Boka Kotorska and Primorje and that part of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you aware, Mr. Samardzic, of any special status that may have been afforded to the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: In the 14 centuries of the existence of the Croatian and pan-Slavic town of Dubrovnik, no armed force had attacked it, or waged a campaign against the old walls of Dubrovnik. Powerful armies, starting from the Byzantine empire, the British empire, the Russian empire, the Venetian republic, not even Hitler's Germany or fascist Germany [as interpreted], ever tried to conduct war operations in Dubrovnik. Unfortunately, it was only Montenegro who had this honour, and I am deeply ashamed of this, as a Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to request the usher to distribute a document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just add: When the French occupied the Dubrovnik Republic, they did so without any military operations, because they didn't want to deface the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have just been reminded by my colleague that there may have been an error in the transcript on page 65, line 19, where it is believed that the reference was not even Hitler's Germany or fascist Italy, I believe it was taken down as Germany, and if that -- if I am correct by checking, I would ask for a redaction in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, in front of you is a document bearing the date of 5 October 1991 and an endorsement by an individual named Dragutin Zelenovic. Can you tell us, if you know, who is Dragutin Zelenovic, or was?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Dragutin Zelenovic was the prime minister of Serbia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And the document, which is addressed to the government of the Republic of Croatia, Zagreb, indicates that the government of the Republic of Serbia, on its session held on 4 October 1991, has been acquainted with the danger to the civilian population in the city of Dubrovnik that represent a part of the Serbian and Croatian history, as well as a magnificent monument of the world cultural heritage. I think there's a typo in the word "world" in English. "Your decision to install paramilitary units, black legions and numerous foreign mercenaries in a city of invaluable historical and cultural value and to launch an armed attack on settlements in Herzegovina and Boka Kotorska from this position represents a totally uncivilised, inhuman, and undignified act. We hope that you yourself are aware of this and that you will use all the force at your disposal to stop destruction of Dubrovnik, in order for it not to be destroyed as other cities. Addressing you with this letter to stop the destruction of Dubrovnik, the government of the Republic of Serbia expresses its firm conviction that all the members of the Yugoslavian army and troops of the Territorial Defence will put all the efforts to protect this historical town." There is -- first of all, are you familiar with the content of this letter?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I saw this letter a long time ago. Croatia published it very soon, and it shows the enormous cynicism of the Serbian prime minister, a cynicism equal to that of Goebbels's. He says that the JNA, that is, the prime minister of Serbia says, that the JNA and the Territorial Defence - he's referring to the TO of Montenegro - will save Dubrovnik from the Croats. And at the same time, as is evident here, he says that they will prevent attacks on Herzegovina and Boka Kotorska. But it was evident that no such attacks were taking place. This in fact is an attempt to justify the aggression on Dubrovnik, and this justification is being put forward by no less a person than the prime minister of Serbia, trying to blame Montenegro and the JNA for everything. He was one of Slobodan Milosevic's men, and were it not tragic, it would be ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know if at the time there were persons from the Republic of Serbia in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, there were people who had been mobilised in the units. I don't think too many, though. The units were mostly composed of Montenegrins and people from Herzegovina who took part in the operations around Dubrovnik. I assume there were people from Serbia too. I can't say how many. The army must have mobilised them, but to the best of my knowledge, most of those who fought there were from Montenegro and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The references to the city of invaluable historical and cultural value that are in this particular document, do you know or do you recall whether or not there was any discussion at the meeting you attended on October 1st as to the invaluable historical and cultural value of the city of Dubrovnik? Did that factor into that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: You mean the meeting that was held on the 1st of October?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Well, this was said at the meeting, and I think General Strugar did say that everything would be done to avoid destruction, to avoid destruction to the extent possible. He did not specify anything about the historic monuments or anything, but he referred to general destruction, and he said that they would try to end the campaign as soon as possible. But not in the sense that Zelenovic is talking about here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P29.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was your -- what were your views on any conflict that may have been between the JNA forces and the Croatian forces, in particular, in the Dubrovnik area? Actually, let us restrict it to the Dubrovnik area. What was your view?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: After the meeting on the 1st of October, the same evening when I came back home, it was clear to me that this was no defence matter, that there would be an attack on Dubrovnik, probably the next day. I knew this was an act of aggression, and I was deeply disappointed. I was disappointed that we were the ones to attack Dubrovnik. When we had lived for so long in brotherhood and friendship, an unjust war was being waged. And I stated this quite clearly in my activities, until I was removed from my position as foreign minister for Montenegro. The first evening, I was perplexed. My statement was that we should indeed defend ourselves if we had been attacked. I believe General Strugar, believing that his words would not be untrue. However, the same evening, or the next day, it was clear to me that this was an unjust act of aggression or war against a people that had not harmed us in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were your views generally known among your colleagues in the government and in the parliament?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I made my position very clear. I made my position public. Especially I pointed out in public, on the 17th of October, in the evening, on earlier occasions too, but the 17th of October is particularly important because I spoke during a session of the Montenegrin assembly, when Lord Carrington's plan was on the discussion. That was probably the last chance to stop the war. Lord Carrington's plan envisaged a complete ceasefire and a large degree of autonomy for the Serbs in Croatia. According to what Lord Carrington said himself at the conference, there was fear that Croatia would not play along with this. However, Slobodan Milosevic's policies at the time were to refuse Lord Carrington's plan, to turn it down, so the war was waged on with even greater ferocity. Now that I've referred to the 17th of October, I must point out that even back then it was clear to everyone that the operations around Dubrovnik would not go as smoothly as has been promised initially.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Taking you back for a moment: Did you know an individual named Kristo Djurovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Captain Kristo Djurovic. It's a naval rank equivalent to colonel. He was the commander of the military naval district of Boka Kotorska. Now that we've mentioned him, 10 or 15 days before the hostilities, the 1st of October, he came to see me at my office at Jugooceanija, in Kotor, and he was extremely worried. He told me that a war would be launched against Croatia, of which he -- in which he did not wish to take part. I refused to believe him, although there were people who were telling me before the war that there would be a war very soon, Hrvoje Kacic, Djurovic, Henri Wejnaendts. I refused to believe any of these people that what eventually happened would happen. Kristo Djurovic was killed. No light was shed on the exact circumstances of his death. He died in fighting. I knew him to be an honest man and that he refused to take part in fighting against Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was his nationality, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. He did not die in fighting.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know his nationality. He was Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But against the -- against fighting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: He was a Montenegrin, but very much in favour of brotherhood with the Croatian people, the Serbian people, and all the peoples of the former Yugoslavia, and that was the spirit that he had been raised in. That was the only way he was taught to think. We have two cases in Montenegro that I was aware of. Admiral Barovic committed suicide in order to avoid taking part in the war in Croatia. He killed himself. Kristo Djurovic was killed, under circumstances of which we know nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated he was killed. Who was he succeeded by? Who was his successor?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic was appointed as his successor, who had up to that point been the defence minister of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have any reason to speak to General Strugar during the course of the campaign?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. It so happened that once during the campaign - I think it was in early November. I can't remember the exact date - three British persons came to see me who had been sent by the authorities to go and see me, and asked me to put them in touch with General Strugar. There was no way for me to do that, nor did I know his whereabouts. I spoke to Pavle Bulatovic, to see if he could put me in touch with General Strugar, or rather, to act as some kind of liaison for the British officers, who requested to meet General Strugar. Pavle did everything within his power, and he established a link between my office and the front line. Admiral Jokic was the one who answered the phone. I didn't personally speak to General Strugar, but Jokic told me the following: Standing next to me is General Strugar. And he said that General Strugar could not see the British officers on the front line but that he would be glad to see them once he was back in Podgorica. That was the conversation we had over the phone, the conversation with Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have any difficulty with the telephone communication? Was it a clear communication?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: It was quite clear. Admiral Jokic went on to speak about something else immediately. He wasn't really interested in what those British officers were after. Obviously, things were not going the way they wanted them to go on the front line, and Admiral Jokic started asking me about my opinion. This is what he said, exactly: Captain - because that was the way he addressed me. I had the rank of captain, the naval rank - "Captain, General Strugar and I want your opinion on this. Can we organise a Dubrovnik republic?" And I said: "No, General. Under no circumstances. Leave this well alone. No one in the wide world will stand by and watch you establish any kind of Dubrovnik Republic, not as part of Serbia, not as an independent state. Under no circumstances whatsoever. You are completely deluded." That's what I told him. That's what I told the admiral, and I suppose he conveyed my message to General Strugar in this conversation. Just by way of clarification: At this time, all the media, all the printed media and the television - we're talking about the establishment of the Dubrovnik Republic - the members of the national party of Montenegro had been given the job of helping of authorities to establish a Dubrovnik Republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have any additional conversations with General Strugar while there was fighting going on in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please. Please. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is: Did you have any additional conversations with General Strugar. Another conversation. Which was the first conversation? There was no first conversation. Please. The witness said who exactly he talked to, so how can we now have a question like this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can rephrase it so that it's indicated that General Strugar was the object of the conversation through the intermediary, Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have a conversation with Admiral Jokic in which the witness made some assumption about the presence of General Strugar, is the way I understand the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I think it goes higher than that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you make any other attempts to reach General Strugar during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't. That was the first and only time I talked to Jokic, and I'll repeat. He said, standing next to me is General Strugar. We both want your opinion. These were the exact words he used: We want your opinion on the possibility of organising a Dubrovnik Republic. My answer was: Under no circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say the first and only time you talked to Admiral Jokic, do you mean in connection with being near a front?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, near a front. I didn't make any phone calls to the front, to anyone, not to General Strugar and not to Admiral Jokic. The things took their course, natural course, and I had no further contact with them. The war situation was worsening. Suddenly it was the 6th of December, and I had other business given to me by the government, but I had no further conversations with Admiral Jokic since. I knew Admiral Jokic from before. We did meet a number of times, not too many times, but we did meet several times. Prior to becoming defence minister of Serbia, he had served in Boka Kotorska, and that was where we met. But I never met General Strugar. I knew of him. I respected him. But I had no personal contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was your understanding of how the conflict in Dubrovnik was going? Was it perceived as successful?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: That's what the propaganda said. However, it was a huge defeat for the JNA. It was a huge defeat for Slobodan Milosevic's policy. It was perfectly clear that perhaps Dubrovnik could have been taken by military means but that the international community and Dubrovnik's defence were strong enough, I mean the influence of the international community and the town's defence were strong enough to repel any attacks. One way or another, Dubrovnik would have been defended, and successfully defended, in the end. This was a -- this spelled a defeat for Slobodan Milosevic's policy and the course of action pursued by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the morale of the Croatian side, the mood, the morale?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: The morale. I was not in contact with the Croatian military, but what was clear, what you could see, is that the Croats were fighting. They were defending themselves from aggression. Of course, the morale was quite high on the Croatian side, especially in the area around Dubrovnik. They were defending the town. There is nothing else to say about this. Hrvoje Kacic was a Croatian official. He could have spirited his son away so that his son would not have to take part in the fighting, and yet he sent him to the front, to defend Dubrovnik from this aggression and from this war. But there were other such examples, numerous.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us anything about the morale of the soldiers from Montenegro, and perhaps if you know anything about other JNA force morale?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I don't think the morale of the soldiers from Montenegro was much, especially in view of the fact that a large number of soldiers were allowed to loot, to torch. You can hardly speak of morale in situations like that. What was being done -- what was being done in Konavle was a great shame for the JNA, it's an ignominy for Montenegro. The morale was certainly low. I do not hereby wish to say that all the soldiers who were on the Dubrovnik front were like that, that all of them were looting and committing crimes. However, the best part of them did commit these acts, and this shame, this blemish, will stay on the face of Montenegro forever. Acts of looting were carried out. First the local population had fled to the town of Dubrovnik itself from the area, and then the soldiers would come and loot the houses. In order to cover their tracks, they would just burn -- they would just set fire to the houses and torch the houses. If you look at the photographs of Konavle after the houses had been torched, the area looks frightening, terrifying. There were bands, groups of soldiers, marauding the area, taking things away from houses and taking them back to Montenegro. So there were individual crimes being committed, but it was also organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. May I ask you, though: Let's return to Dubrovnik. Do you know if -- or the nature of the weaponry that was available to forces under the JNA? In other words, do you know what type of weapons?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: They had all the weapons that the JNA had. The JNA was a well-equipped army. It was, in terms of its strength, probably the third strongest or the fourth strongest army in Europe. They had tanks. They had modern weapons, helicopters, cannon, and all of this was used in the Dubrovnik theatre of war. They were certainly not short of ammunition or weapons, and this was used against Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know how close the weapons came to the city of Dubrovnik? That's part one. And then, if you're able to tell us, how close, if you know, weapons may have come to the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: I can only judge on the basis of reports and TV coverage. It was very close. What was shown on TV, it was within a stone's throw of the Old Town. There were artillery weapons being used to target Dubrovnik, and at the same time, Dubrovnik was being targeted from the sea, from ships. It was all around the town. However, the JNA never entered the town itself. Rijeka Dubrovacka, for example, which is a suburb of Dubrovnik, the JNA held Rijeka Dubrovacka at one point and were about to enter Gruz. So that Dubrovnik was completely surrounded from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Returning for one moment to the question of morale. Are you aware -- were there ever any desertions brought to your attention, desertions brought by forces under the JNA control?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes. I can testify about the following two cases which occurred. I can personally testify about this. A group of 15 or 20 soldiers came to see me at my office in Podgorica who had deserted from the front. They had fled the front. And they asked my assistance in helping them to get away from the military police. They knew about my political convictions and they asked me to help them. I was in no position to save their hides, obviously, but what I advised them to do was to go back home and lie low until the whole thing blew over. Another case of desertion, another group of between 15 to 20 soldiers had come from the front straight to my office at Jugooceanija, telling me that they refused to fight against Croatia and to fight against Dubrovnik, because those people had never harmed them in any way. They told me about the situation on the front, how they had spent the whole night in the rain with no tents to use. So there were a number of these things happening. On the other hand, you did have large numbers of people who were willing to fight, who were eager to fight, because they believed Yugoslavia was in danger. They had been misled by propaganda. They sincerely believed that the Ustasha would attack us and that we should defend ourselves. So the overwhelming majority of those soldiers obeyed order from their command. They were there on the front, after all. And yet there was a lot of discontent felt by soldiers on the front. There was no way to disguise this fact. I know that Momir Bulatovic reviewed troops and spoke to the troops and he said whoever wishes to leave may do so now. And a number of soldiers did leave, who at that time refused to fight. There were case of resistance in Montenegro. Therefore, you can't say that all the Montenegrins attacked Dubrovnik. There were many, many Montenegrins who were against the war, who were against attacking Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did there come a point in time where it may have appeared that the goals of the campaign could not be achieved?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, there were some negotiations. There were ceasefires, cessation of hostilities, on a temporary basis, and it became obvious that Dubrovnik could not be taken just like that, without great damage done to the international reputation of the former Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia, as such, no longer existed at the time. But I'm talking about potential damage to the people who were then in power. It became clear that it wasn't possible to avoid massive destruction of the town of Dubrovnik itself, unless hostilities ceased. So as far as I remember, hostilities did cease for a while, and were then, after a period of time, resumed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know what the attitude of military leadership was toward ceasing hostilities in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: For me to say specifically what their attitude was, I don't think I can. I believe that for a while they complied with the ceasefire, but then resumed military operations after a certain time. What exactly their considerations were, I can't say, but there was a cessation of hostilities for a while, not for too long, I believe. At that time, Hrvoje Kacic flew over to Titograd for negotiations but was not successful, because no generals and no representatives of the Montenegrin authorities were willing to receive him, to see him. Therefore, I can't say anything specific about the attitudes of the military leaders. I can only tell you about what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know, perhaps, or was it brought to your attention, the attitude of Minister of Defence, Bozidar Babic, about cessation of hostilities, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Bozidar Babic is a general. I think he became a general then. He was very nationalistic and he said that one should fight to the end. I don't think, however, that he was particularly influential in the army. I was not really privy to military circles; therefore, I was in no position to know. His rhetoric was very nationalistic, and he expressed great hate, hatred, for the Ustasha. He was one of the hawks, one of the people who incited others to keep on fighting to final victory. However, when it became clear that defeat was imminent, he calmed down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know of a person named Bozidar Vucurevic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know the person. I only met him once, when he came to Titograd.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who was he? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: He was a lorry driver, a driver, who came to the forefront during the operation around Dubrovnik, and later he became mayor of the town of Trebinje. He is a hard-liner, a hawk.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where is Trebinje? Where is Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Trebinje is a town north/north-east of Dubrovnik. The distance is 24 kilometres. There's a local road that takes you from Dubrovnik to Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, is this a convenient time, or is there something you'd like to finish?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I could just finish on the subject of Mr. Vucurevic, then I would be -- I would ask to break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any particular attitude that Mr. Vucurevic held toward Dubrovnik, and particularly during the time of this conflict?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Regrettably, he was familiar with the fact that there would be an attack, and he was making jokes about it, that he would be in Dubrovnik to have coffee on the 1st of October, on the main street. The mayor of Dubrovnik, Petar Poljanic, can confirm this. He said he was the tourism person and would run tourism the way he saw fit and when he saw fit. It was in this sense that he developed his own political activity as a half-literate peasant who was suddenly was given an opportunity to attack Dubrovnik and to demolish it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you mentioned he would run tourism, what would be his relationship to tourism? Why did you mention that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: To target the hotels whenever he saw fit. That's probably what he had in mind, to destroy Dubrovnik. He displayed obvious hatred of Dubrovnik. He was one of those who, on many an occasion, displayed hatred for Dubrovnik, and he used every possible opportunity to show that his time had now come. He was an advocate of Chetnik ideology of the Greater Serbia. He said that the Ustasha should be punished, and that's what he based his activity around Dubrovnik on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say - and I will finish with this particular theme - when you say that he -- let me just make sure. I'll read it back. You mentioned hotels, to target the hotels whenever he saw fit. Can you explain that? What did you mean by that, and what would be the impact of doing something like that? Why would you have made that comment?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: He simply hated Dubrovnik. He couldn't bear the fact that people from Dubrovnik had a personal income of $15,000 per capita, which in his case was as little as 500 or 300 dollars. So this was the reason he hated Dubrovnik, with all his might, which he showed very clearly. He said he would build an even older Dubrovnik, a new one but even older. Those were the words he used. This was the well-known old Chetnik nationalistic propaganda. He was deeply convinced that his time had come, that the time had come for him and the likes of him, and he acted accordingly. It was well known how he baptised Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzic, do you know how far or what the distance is between Trebinje and Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA SAMARDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. 24 kilometres. A local road, not a bad one, had been built in the former Yugoslavia, and people from Trebinje went to the beach in Dubrovnik. It was a day-trip for them. It was just a short hop. It was quite usual for people from Trebinje to have coffee in Dubrovnik on the main street, and the two towns were well-connected. People from Trebinje felt that Dubrovnik was also theirs, in a way. Many of them worked in Dubrovnik and drove back home the same day. Now there's nothing like that going on any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. We will have to ask you to come back tomorrow, Mr. Samardzic. We will be adjourning now for the evening. Was there any matter that needed to be raised, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. Our expert was working today, and the way in which this work was organised is such that she has succeeded and completed most of her tasks. There are still things that remain to be done tomorrow; however, that would only require 45 minutes more than you said the other day when we discussed this. Therefore, we would request, if possible, that the hearing tomorrow commence at 1500 hours and not at a quarter past 2.00. These 45 minutes would suffice for us to complete all the necessary procedures concerning the medical examination of our client. This is our request. We don't think it's a particularly ambitious request, and we do not believe that this would jeopardise the course of our work here in Court. That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you give an indication of how long your cross-examination of the present witness is likely to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it will certainly not be longer than the examination-in-chief by the OTP. It may well prove shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it help you to know how much more we have to go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There are I think another three to four exhibits, one of which is a video, lasting -- I'll be conservative, two to three, plus a video. The video runs approximately -- we won't have it run its whole time. I'm afraid Ms. McCreath said 30 minutes. I don't think so. But -- and then a bit more of examination to accompany it, but I don't anticipate, other than whatever time it needs to present the exhibits, I do not anticipate a lot of additional material to be brought up. Redirect would, of course, just simply depend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would seem unlikely, then, that we could be confident of finishing the witness tomorrow. That's my concern. Whatever time we started, given the time that has gone already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In view of the unusual situation, we are prepared to accept your request, Mr. Petrovic, that there should be a delayed start tomorrow, commencing at 3.00 rather than 2.15. May we encourage you to try, in view of that - you or Mr. Rodic, whichever it will be - to conclude the cross-examination in the course of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your understanding, Your Honour. We'll do our best to do as you have just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, then. We will adjourn until 3.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 21st day of January 2004, at 3.00 p.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.05 p.m.
